description: Cross-provider cloud architecture (AWS / Azure / GCP service mapping, identity, networking, storage, cost trade-offs) plus the hardware under it: CPUs, GPUs/TPUs, AI cluster networking and datacenters. For platform and enterprise architects who design on more than one cloud.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Shared responsibility model: what does the provider secure, and what does the customer secure?
notes.back:
Provider: security of the cloud (facilities, hardware, hypervisor).
Customer: security in the cloud (data, identities, configuration, workloads).
notes.extra: Shift: the line moves toward the provider as you go IaaS → PaaS → SaaS/serverless. Same principle on all three clouds.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed (PaaS/serverless) vs self-run (IaaS): what do you gain and what do you pay?
notes.back:
Gain: less ops, built-in scaling/patching/high availability (HA), faster delivery.
Pay: higher unit cost, less control, tighter lock-in.
notes.analogy: Renting a furnished, serviced flat vs owning a house: someone else fixes the boiler, but you can't knock down walls and the rent is higher.
notes.extra: In practice: the decision rarely hinges on compute price; it hinges on the engineering time the managed service removes.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: What primarily drives cloud vendor lock-in (not compute)?
notes.back: The differentiated managed services you build on (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, BigQuery, identity and access management (IAM), eventing) and data gravity: egress fees make moving large datasets expensive.
notes.analogy: Data gravity: a large dataset is like a planet; services, apps and more data fall into its orbit, and escaping costs energy (egress).
notes.extra: Mitigations, each with a cost: open formats (Parquet/Delta), containers + Kubernetes, Terraform, provider software development kits (SDKs) behind interfaces.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Multi-cloud: when does it actually pay off?
notes.back: Regulatory/sovereignty mandates, negotiating leverage, a best-of-breed service on another cloud (e.g. BigQuery next to an AWS app), and M&A reality.
notes.extra: Pragmatic default: one primary cloud; stay portable at the boundaries (containers, Terraform, open formats).

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Multi-cloud: what are its main hidden costs?
notes.back: Doubled ops and skills, lowest-common-denominator architecture, cross-cloud egress, weaker volume discounts, and a larger security surface.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Kubernetes as a portability layer: what does it equalize across Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)/Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)/Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)?
notes.back: Scheduling, the deployment model and in-cluster service networking. Workloads defined as manifests move fairly cleanly.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Kubernetes as a portability layer: where does portability leak?
notes.back: At every cloud integration: storage (container storage interface (CSI) drivers), load balancers/ingress, identity and access management (IAM) / workload identity, and the managed databases and queues the apps depend on.
notes.analogy: Kubernetes is a universal power adapter: the plug fits every country, but the voltage (storage, IAM, LBs) still differs behind the wall.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Region vs Availability Zone: what failure does spreading across each protect against?
notes.back:
Across AZs (separate datacenters with own power/cooling/network, low-latency linked): a datacenter failure → high availability (HA).
Across regions (separate geographies): a regional disaster → disaster recovery (DR), plus data residency.
notes.analogy: AZs are separate buildings on one campus; regions are separate cities.
notes.extra: GCP calls AZs zones. HA default: ≥ 2–3 AZs in one region.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: Which cloud leans most 'global' in its resource model, and what are examples?
notes.back: GCP: global virtual private cloud (VPC), one global anycast IP for Cloud Load Balancing, multi-region buckets. AWS/Azure stay mostly regional (AWS exceptions: identity and access management (IAM), Route 53, CloudFront).
notes.extra: Trade-off: global resources simplify multi-region but widen the blast radius and complicate data-residency control.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::01 Cloud Models, Regions & Trade-offs
notes.front: VM live migration during host maintenance: what does it do, and why does it matter for stateful VMs?
notes.back: Moves a running VM to another host with no reboot, so host maintenance doesn't interrupt long-running stateful VMs. Without it, maintenance means a scheduled reboot or stop/start.
notes.extra: Example: GCP Compute Engine live-migrates by default; AWS/Azure often need a reboot or stop/start for some maintenance events.

notes.text:
Identity & access management
AWS: {{c1::IAM}}
Azure: {{c2::Microsoft Entra ID (identity) + Azure RBAC (authorization)}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud IAM}}
notes.extra: Azure splits identity (Entra ID: users, groups, apps) from authorization (RBAC role assignments on scopes).

notes.front: Which cloud's identity and access management (IAM) does not inherit permissions down a resource hierarchy, and what does it use for org-wide limits instead?
notes.back: AWS. Policies attach to users, roles or resources only; Organizations service control policies (SCPs) act as guardrails.
notes.extra: Azure RBAC and GCP IAM both inherit down management group/subscription/resource group (RG) or org/folder/project.

notes.front: In cloud identity and access management (IAM) policy evaluation, what wins when an Allow and a Deny both match?
notes.back: The explicit Deny. Default is implicit deny; an Allow only applies if no Deny matches.
notes.extra: Same rule in AWS IAM, Azure RBAC deny assignments and GCP IAM deny policies.

notes.front: In a hierarchical identity and access management (IAM) model, what is a role binding/assignment, and how far does it reach?
notes.back: A role granted to a principal on a node of the resource hierarchy (org, folder/management group, project/subscription, resource). It is inherited by everything below that node.
notes.extra: Examples: GCP IAM bindings; Azure RBAC role assignments on a scope.

notes.text: Primary isolation and billing boundary: AWS {{c1::Account}} · Azure {{c2::Subscription}} · GCP {{c3::Project}}
notes.extra: Best practice everywhere: many small boundaries (per team/env), grouped by AWS Organizations / Azure Management Groups / GCP Folders.

notes.text:
Resource hierarchy, top to bottom:
AWS: {{c1::Organization → OU → Account → Resource}}
Azure: {{c2::Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource}}
GCP: {{c3::Organization → Folder → Project → Resource}}
notes.extra:
Azure's Resource Group is mandatory (every resource lives in exactly one) and has no AWS/GCP equivalent.
Acronyms: OU = organizational unit.

notes.text:
Org-wide permission guardrails
AWS: {{c1::Service Control Policies (SCPs)}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure Policy + RBAC deny assignments}}
GCP: {{c3::Organization Policy constraints}}
notes.extra: SCPs set the maximum permissions: they never grant, only bound.

notes.text:
Workload identity without static keys
AWS: {{c1::IAM roles (IRSA / EKS Pod Identity on EKS)}}
Azure: {{c2::Managed Identities / Workload Identity}}
GCP: {{c3::Service accounts + Workload Identity}}
notes.extra:
All three let pods/VMs assume an identity from the platform instead of embedding long-lived credentials.
Acronyms: IRSA = identity and access management (IAM) roles for service accounts; EKS = Elastic Kubernetes Service.

notes.text:
Secrets management
AWS: {{c1::Secrets Manager (+ Parameter Store)}}
Azure: {{c2::Key Vault}}
GCP: {{c3::Secret Manager}}
notes.extra: Key Vault also holds keys and certificates; AWS keeps keys separately in Key Management Service (KMS).

notes.front: Encryption at rest: what is the default on all three clouds, and what does a customer-managed key (CMK) add?
notes.back: Default: encrypted with platform-managed keys. CMK (AWS KMS / Key Vault / Cloud KMS) adds control, revocation and audit.
notes.extra:
Pitfall: with CMK, key availability = data availability. Delete or lose access to the key and the data is gone.
Acronyms: KMS = Key Management Service.

notes.text:
Confidential computing (data encrypted in use)
AWS: {{c1::Nitro Enclaves}}
Azure: {{c2::Confidential VMs / confidential containers}}
GCP: {{c3::Confidential VMs (AMD SEV / Intel TDX)}}
notes.extra:
Protects memory even from the hypervisor and host operator.
Acronyms: TDX = Trust Domain Extensions; SEV = Secure Encrypted Virtualization.

notes.front: AWS virtual private cloud (VPC) / Azure virtual network (VNet) vs GCP VPC: what is the scope difference, and why does it matter?
notes.back: AWS VPC and Azure VNet are regional; a GCP VPC is global (subnets regional). Multi-region on AWS/Azure needs peering or a transit hub; on GCP it is one network.
notes.extra: Trade-off: simpler global topology vs a single larger fault and policy domain. Stitching tools: AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN.

notes.front: Cloud firewall primitives: which cloud adds a second, stateless layer, and what is it?
notes.back: AWS: Network access control lists (ACLs) at subnet level, on top of stateful Security Groups. Azure network security groups (NSGs) and GCP virtual private cloud (VPC) firewall rules are stateful only.
notes.extra: Stateless = you must allow return traffic explicitly. GCP firewall rules target network tags or service accounts, not network interface cards (NICs).

notes.text:
Private service connectivity (service as private endpoint in your network)
AWS: {{c1::PrivateLink}}
Azure: {{c2::Private Link}}
GCP: {{c3::Private Service Connect}}

Dedicated private line to on-prem
AWS: {{c1::Direct Connect}}
Azure: {{c2::ExpressRoute}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Interconnect}}
notes.extra: Bypasses the public internet for bandwidth, predictable latency and compliance.

notes.text:
Load balancers:
AWS: {{c1::ALB (L7), NLB (L4)}}
Azure: {{c2::Application Gateway (L7, regional), Load Balancer (L4), Front Door (L7, global)}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Load Balancing, one product, global or regional, L4/L7}}
notes.extra:
GCP's global layer 7 (L7) load balancer (LB) behind a single anycast IP is its distinctive feature.
Acronyms: L4 = layer 4; ALB = Application Load Balancer; NLB = Network Load Balancer.

notes.text:
content delivery network (CDN)
AWS: {{c1::CloudFront}}
Azure: {{c2::Front Door (also global L7 LB + WAF)}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud CDN}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: L7 = layer 7; LB = load balancer; WAF = web application firewall.

notes.text:
Managed DNS
AWS: {{c1::Route 53}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure DNS (+ Traffic Manager for routing)}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud DNS}}
notes.extra: Route 53 combines DNS with health-checked routing policies in one service.

notes.front: Managed (provider-branded) service meshes: what is the durable pattern behind the churn?
notes.back: Provider-branded meshes come and go; Istio is the common substrate underneath and the Kubernetes Gateway API the converging surface. Design against those, not the brand.
notes.extra: Examples: AWS App Mesh retired (→ VPC Lattice / Elastic Container Service (ECS) Service Connect); Azure Open Service Mesh retired (→ Istio-based Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) add-on); GCP Cloud Service Mesh is managed Istio.

notes.text:
IaaS virtual machines
AWS: {{c1::EC2}}
Azure: {{c2::Virtual Machines}}
GCP: {{c3::Compute Engine}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: EC2 = Elastic Compute Cloud.

notes.text:
Functions as a Service
AWS: {{c1::Lambda}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure Functions}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions)}}

Serverless containers (no node management)
AWS: {{c1::Fargate (ECS or EKS)}}
Azure: {{c2::Container Apps / Container Instances}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Run}}
notes.extra:
Cloud Run is request-driven containers with scale-to-zero, a middle ground between function as a service (FaaS) and full orchestration.
Acronyms: EKS = Elastic Kubernetes Service; ECS = Elastic Container Service.

notes.text:
Managed Kubernetes
AWS: {{c1::EKS}}
Azure: {{c2::AKS}}
GCP: {{c3::GKE}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: EKS = Elastic Kubernetes Service; AKS = Azure Kubernetes Service; GKE = Google Kubernetes Engine.

notes.front: Managed Kubernetes cost: what do you pay for besides the worker nodes?
notes.back: A control-plane fee per cluster-hour (sometimes waived on a free tier whose paid tier adds an uptime service level agreement (SLA)), plus load balancers, storage and egress. Many small clusters multiply the fixed fee.
notes.extra: Examples: Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) ~$0.10 per cluster-hour; Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) a management fee with a free-tier credit for one cluster; Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Free tier (Standard adds the SLA). Rates drift; the structure is the durable fact.

notes.front: Node-less (fully managed node) mode of a managed Kubernetes service vs standard node pools: what do you give up?
notes.back: The provider runs and sizes the nodes; you pay per pod resource request. You lose node-level freedom: privileged pods, some DaemonSets, custom node config and kernel tuning.
notes.extra: Examples: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot, Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Fargate profiles, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Automatic / virtual nodes (Azure Container Instances, ACI).

notes.text:
Container registry
AWS: {{c1::ECR}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure Container Registry}}
GCP: {{c3::Artifact Registry}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: ECR = Elastic Container Registry.

notes.text:
Native infrastructure as code
AWS: {{c1::CloudFormation (+ CDK)}}
Azure: {{c2::ARM templates → Bicep}}
GCP: {{c3::Infrastructure Manager (Terraform-based)}}
notes.extra:
Terraform/OpenTofu is the cross-cloud default regardless.
Acronyms: CDK = Cloud Development Kit.

notes.text:
Metrics & logs
AWS: {{c1::CloudWatch}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure Monitor (Log Analytics + Application Insights)}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Monitoring / Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver)}}

notes.front: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?
notes.back: Type 1 (bare-metal: kernel-based virtual machine (KVM), ESXi, Hyper-V) runs directly on hardware; Type 2 runs as an app on a host OS (VirtualBox). Clouds use Type 1.

notes.text: {{c1::KVM}} is a Linux kernel module that turns Linux into a Type 1 hypervisor; it underpins OpenStack and most public clouds.
notes.extra: AWS Nitro and GCP both run kernel-based virtual machine (KVM)-derived hypervisors.

notes.front: When do you pick a bare-metal instance over a virtualized one?
notes.back: When you need the whole server without hypervisor overhead or limits: GPU-heavy AI, licensing tied to physical cores, nested virtualization, or hardware features (perf counters).

notes.front: Why do clouds oversubscribe CPU and network, and what is the symptom when the bet fails?
notes.back: They sell more virtual capacity than exists, betting tenants rarely peak together. When they do: noisy neighbors (CPU steal time, jitter).
notes.analogy: Airline overbooking: profitable because some passengers never show, painful on the day everyone does.
notes.extra: Burstable instances (AWS T, Azure B) are oversubscription with a credit system.

notes.front: What is bin packing in cluster scheduling, and what does it trade against?
notes.back: Placing workloads onto hosts to maximize utilization within CPU/memory/GPU/affinity constraints. It trades against spreading for resilience: tighter packing = bigger blast radius per node.
notes.analogy: Packing a moving van: Tetris-tight saves trips, but one dropped box takes more with it.

notes.text:
Storage models:
{{c1::Block}}: raw addressable blocks, a virtual disk for one host (EBS)
{{c2::Object}}: immutable objects + metadata over an HTTP API (S3)
{{c3::File}}: shared hierarchical filesystem over the network (NFS/SMB)
notes.extra: Acronyms: EBS = Elastic Block Store; S3 = Simple Storage Service; NFS = network file system; SMB = server message block.

notes.text:
Object storage
AWS: {{c1::S3}}
Azure: {{c2::Blob Storage}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud Storage (GCS)}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: S3 = Simple Storage Service; GCS = Google Cloud Storage.

notes.text:
Block storage for VMs
AWS: {{c1::EBS}}
Azure: {{c2::Managed Disks}}
GCP: {{c3::Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: EBS = Elastic Block Store.

notes.text:
Object storage tiers (hot → archive):
AWS Simple Storage Service (S3): {{c1::Standard → Standard-IA / One Zone-IA → Glacier tiers}}
Azure Blob: {{c2::Hot → Cool → Cold → Archive}}
Google Cloud Storage (GCS): {{c3::Standard → Nearline → Coldline → Archive}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: IA = infrequent access.

notes.front: Storage tiering: what do you pay for moving data to a colder tier?
notes.back: Cheaper per-GB storage in exchange for retrieval fees, higher latency (archive: hours) and minimum storage durations (early-delete charges).
notes.extra: Lifecycle policies automate moves by age or last access.

notes.front: Are cloud object stores (Simple Storage Service (S3), Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage (GCS)) eventually consistent?
notes.back: No. All three are strongly read-after-write consistent for all operations (S3 since December 2020; Blob Storage and GCS earlier).
notes.extra: Older interview answers calling S3 eventually consistent are outdated.

notes.front: Hard disk drive (HDD) vs SSD: what is the physical difference and its main consequence?
notes.back: HDD: spinning platters + moving head → milliseconds of seek per random I/O. SSD: flash, no moving parts → microsecond latency and far higher random input/output operations per second (IOPS).

notes.front: Why is non-volatile memory express (NVMe) so much faster than Serial ATA (SATA) for SSDs?
notes.back: SATA/Advanced Host Controller Interface (AHCI) was designed for spinning disks (one queue, 32 commands). NVMe runs over peripheral component interconnect express (PCIe) lanes with up to 64K queues, giving far higher input/output operations per second (IOPS) and lower latency.

notes.front: What does IOPS measure?
notes.back: Input/output operations per second: how many reads/writes a device or volume handles per second.

notes.front: Input/output operations per second (IOPS) vs throughput: which limit hits a database and which hits a backup or ML data loader?
notes.back: Databases do small random I/O → IOPS-bound. Backups and data loaders stream large sequential reads → throughput (MB/s)-bound.
notes.extra: Cloud volumes cap both separately (e.g. Elastic Block Store (EBS) gp3 provisions IOPS and MB/s independently).

notes.front: Why do distributed object stores use erasure coding instead of 3× replication or redundant array of independent disks (RAID)?
notes.back: Erasure coding (e.g. 6 data + 3 parity) survives several lost fragments at ~1.5× overhead vs 3× for replication, and spans nodes/zones, not one server's disks like RAID.
notes.extra: Cost: more CPU and network for reads during failures and for rebuilds. RAID 5 survives only one disk and has risky rebuild windows on large drives.

notes.front: SAN vs NAS?
notes.back:
Storage area network (SAN): dedicated network giving servers block access (Fibre Channel, Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI)).
Network-attached storage (NAS): file-level access over the normal network (network file system (NFS), server message block (SMB)); simpler, usually slower.

notes.front: What is Ceph, and where do you meet it?
notes.back: Open-source distributed storage offering object, block and file from one cluster. Common backend for OpenStack and on-prem Kubernetes (Rook).

notes.front: Why is storage often the bottleneck in AI training?
notes.back: GPUs consume data faster than storage can feed it, so they idle. Fixes: parallel filesystems (Lustre, General Parallel File System (GPFS)), local non-volatile memory express (NVMe) caching, sharded datasets with prefetch.

notes.text:
Managed relational database
AWS: {{c1::RDS + Aurora}}
Azure: {{c2::Azure SQL Database, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL}}
GCP: {{c3::Cloud SQL + AlloyDB}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: RDS = Relational Database Service.

notes.text:
Managed NoSQL key-value / document
AWS: {{c1::DynamoDB}}
Azure: {{c2::Cosmos DB}}
GCP: {{c3::Firestore (document), Bigtable (wide-column)}}

Cloud data warehouse
AWS: {{c1::Redshift}}
Azure: {{c2::Microsoft Fabric (successor to Synapse)}}
GCP: {{c3::BigQuery}}

Point-to-point message queue
AWS: {{c1::SQS}}
Azure: {{c2::Service Bus}}
GCP: {{c3::Pub/Sub (+ Cloud Tasks)}}
notes.extra: Acronyms: SQS = Simple Queue Service.

notes.text:
High-throughput event stream
AWS: {{c1::Kinesis Data Streams}}
Azure: {{c2::Event Hubs (Kafka-compatible)}}
GCP: {{c3::Pub/Sub}}
notes.extra: GCP uses Pub/Sub for both queueing and streaming.

notes.front: What do Aurora and AlloyDB change compared with vanilla managed Postgres (Relational Database Service (RDS) / Cloud SQL)?
notes.back: They split compute from a purpose-built distributed storage layer (Aurora: 6 copies across 3 availability zones (AZs)), giving faster failover and cheap read replicas. AlloyDB adds columnar acceleration.
notes.analogy: Instead of each server carrying its own filing cabinet, all servers share one replicated archive; replacing a server no longer means copying the cabinet.

notes.front: DynamoDB vs Cosmos DB: how does each go multi-region, and how much consistency choice do you get?
notes.back:
DynamoDB: regional; Global Tables add multi-active replication (last-writer-wins). Reads: eventual or strong.
Cosmos DB: built-in global distribution with five tunable consistency levels.
notes.extra: Consistency-level details live in the Distributed Systems & Data and AZ-305 decks.

notes.front: BigQuery vs Redshift: core architectural difference?
notes.back:
BigQuery: serverless, storage and compute fully separated, pay per bytes scanned or slots.
Redshift: started as provisioned clusters you size; Redshift Serverless now exists.
notes.extra: BigQuery is the reference no-cluster warehouse.

notes.front: Why is data egress the classic cloud cost trap?
notes.back: Ingress is free but egress to the internet is billed per GB, and cross-region and even cross-availability zone (AZ) traffic is charged. Chatty, multi-region designs leak money invisibly.
notes.analogy: Hotel minibar pricing: checking in is free, everything you take out is billed.
notes.extra: Rough order: internet > cross-region > cross-AZ > same-AZ (often free). Keep traffic local.

notes.text: Spot capacity eviction notice: AWS Spot {{c1::2 minutes}} · Azure Spot VMs {{c2::30 seconds}} · GCP Spot VMs {{c3::30 seconds}}
notes.extra: Up to ~60–90% off. Good for batch and fault-tolerant work; bad for stateful single instances. GCP Spot replaced Preemptible (which had a 24-h cap).

notes.text:
Commitment discounts (1–3 yr)
AWS: {{c1::Reserved Instances + Savings Plans}}
Azure: {{c2::Reservations + Savings Plans}}
GCP: {{c3::Committed Use Discounts (CUDs)}}
notes.extra: Savings Plans commit to $/hour of spend, not a specific instance type, so they survive re-sizing.

notes.front: Commitment-based vs automatic usage-based discounts: what is the difference?
notes.back:
Commitment: you promise 1–3 years of spend or instances and get the discount up front (reservations, savings plans, committed use discounts (CUDs)).
Automatic: the provider discounts resources that run most of the month, with no promise.
notes.extra: Example: GCP Sustained Use Discounts are automatic; AWS/Azure need an explicit reservation or savings plan for comparable discounts.

notes.text:
Custom ARM server CPUs
AWS: {{c1::Graviton}}
Azure: {{c2::Cobalt}}
GCP: {{c3::Axion}}
notes.extra: Typically ~20–40% better price-performance for compatible scale-out workloads.

notes.front: Why compare total cost of ownership (TCO) rather than server or GPU price?
notes.back: Purchase price is a fraction of lifetime cost: power, cooling, network, space, staff and maintenance often dominate.
notes.extra: Cloud vs on-prem comparisons go wrong when one side counts only hardware.

notes.front: Why does capacity planning matter more for GPUs than for general compute?
notes.back: Lead times for GPUs, power and datacenter space run to months, so demand must be forecast and capacity reserved ahead of need.

notes.front: Core vs simultaneous multithreading (SMT) hardware thread (Hyper-Threading): what is shared, and what speedup do you get?
notes.back: A core has its own execution units. SMT runs 2 threads on one core sharing those units: better utilization, typically ~10–30% gain, not 2×.
notes.analogy: One chef with two order tickets: while one dish simmers, he chops for the other, but he is still one chef.

notes.front: What is a vCPU on most x86 cloud instances, and what is the exception?
notes.back: Usually one hyperthread, so 2 vCPU = 1 physical core. On AWS Graviton (no simultaneous multithreading (SMT)) 1 vCPU = 1 full core.
notes.extra: Matters when comparing instance prices or setting K8s CPU requests.

notes.text: CPU caches: {{c1::L1}} is smallest and fastest, per core; {{c2::L3}} is largest and slowest, usually shared across cores.
notes.analogy: L1 is the tools on your desk, L2 the drawer, L3 the shared cupboard, RAM the warehouse down the street.

notes.front: What is NUMA?
notes.back: In multi-socket servers each CPU has local memory it reaches fast; memory attached to another socket is remote and slower (crosses Ultra Path Interconnect (UPI) / Infinity Fabric).
notes.analogy: Each socket has its own fridge; you can raid the neighbor's, but it means walking down the hall.

notes.front: Why pin a process to a non-uniform memory access (NUMA) node?
notes.back: Keeping threads on the node that holds their memory avoids cross-socket traffic and latency spikes, important for databases, Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK) and large VMs.
notes.extra: Kubernetes: Topology Manager + CPU Manager static policy.

notes.front: x86-64 and ARM are two instruction set architectures (ISAs). Why is ARM spreading in the cloud?
notes.back: ARM (RISC) gives better performance per watt and lets providers design their own chips (Graviton, Cobalt, Axion). x86-64 (Intel/AMD) still dominates legacy software.
notes.extra: Pitfall: multi-arch container images are needed before moving workloads.

notes.front: What is TDP, and why do architects care?
notes.back: Thermal Design Power: the sustained heat (watts) a chip is rated to dissipate. It sizes power and cooling per server and rack, and caps sustained clock speed.

notes.front: Why does a branch misprediction cost so much?
notes.back: CPUs pipeline instructions (fetch, decode, execute overlap). On a wrong guess the speculatively executed work is flushed and the pipeline refills: ~15–20 wasted cycles.
notes.extra: Speculative execution is also what Spectre-class side channels exploit, hence the hypervisor mitigations in multi-tenant clouds.

notes.front: Why are GPUs a good fit for neural networks?
notes.back: Thousands of simple cores run the same instruction over many data elements, matching the dense matrix math of neural networks.
notes.analogy: A CPU is a few master craftsmen; a GPU is a stadium of people each doing the same simple sum at once.

notes.text: NVIDIA's execution model, where a {{c1::warp}} of 32 threads executes the same instruction in lockstep on different data, is called {{c2::SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads)}}.
notes.extra: Divergent branches inside a warp serialize, which is why GPU code avoids per-thread branching.

notes.text: The repeated building block of an NVIDIA GPU, holding CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, registers and shared memory, is the {{c1::Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)}}.

notes.front: CUDA cores vs Tensor Cores?
notes.back:
CUDA cores: general scalar FP/INT arithmetic.
Tensor Cores: dedicated matrix multiply-accumulate units at low precision (16-bit floating point (FP16)/brain floating point (BF16)/8-bit floating point (FP8)/8-bit integer (INT8)), where most AI floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) come from.

notes.front: What has to fit in GPU memory (VRAM) during training, and why does it decide the GPU count?
notes.back: Weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations. If they don't fit on one GPU, you must shard the model across several.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: mixed-precision Adam training needs ~16 bytes per parameter before activations.

notes.front: What is HBM, and why do datacenter GPUs use it?
notes.back: High Bandwidth Memory: stacked dynamic random access memory (DRAM) placed next to the GPU die on an interposer, giving TB/s bandwidth (H100 ≈ 3.35 TB/s) that graphics double data rate (GDDR) can't match.

notes.front: Why does memory bandwidth often matter more than raw floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) for AI (especially LLM inference)?
notes.back: Many steps are memory-bound: each weight is read for little compute, so the cores idle waiting for data. Bandwidth sets the speed.
notes.analogy: A fast cook with a slow waiter: dishes per hour is set by the waiter.

notes.front: Peripheral component interconnect express (PCIe) vs NVLink for multi-GPU work?
notes.back: PCIe is the general bus to the CPU (Gen5 x16 ≈ 64 GB/s each way). NVLink is a direct GPU-to-GPU link with many times that (H100: 900 GB/s total).

notes.front: What does NVSwitch add beyond NVLink?
notes.back: A switch chip giving all-to-all NVLink connectivity, so every GPU in the node (or NVL rack) talks to every other at full NVLink bandwidth.
notes.analogy: NVLink is a private road between two houses; NVSwitch is a roundabout connecting every house on the street.

notes.front: What is model parallelism, and when is it required?
notes.back: Splitting a model's layers or tensors across GPUs. Required when the model doesn't fit in one GPU's memory; it costs inter-GPU communication on every step.

notes.front: Data parallelism vs model parallelism?
notes.back:
Data: each GPU holds a full model copy, processes different batches, then all-reduces gradients.
Model (tensor/pipeline): each GPU holds part of the model.
notes.extra: Large-model training combines both (plus sharded optimizer state, e.g. Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO)/fully sharded data parallel (FSDP)).

notes.front: What is mixed-precision training, and why keep some parts in FP32?
notes.back: Most math runs in 16-bit floating point (FP16)/brain floating point (BF16)/8-bit floating point (FP8) for speed and memory; master weights and sensitive reductions stay in 32-bit floating point (FP32) to keep training numerically stable.

notes.front: Brain floating point (BF16) vs 16-bit floating point (FP16): why is BF16 preferred for training?
notes.back: BF16 keeps 32-bit floating point (FP32)'s 8-bit exponent (same range) with fewer mantissa bits, so gradients rarely overflow/underflow and no loss scaling is needed.

notes.front: What is NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)?
notes.back: Hardware partitioning of one GPU (A100/H100) into up to 7 isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute slices.
notes.extra: In Kubernetes each MIG slice appears as its own schedulable resource.

notes.front: GPU passthrough vs virtual GPU (vGPU) vs Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)?
notes.back:
Passthrough: whole GPU to one VM.
vGPU: time-sliced share across VMs.
MIG: hardware-isolated partitions with dedicated memory.
notes.extra: Time-slicing has no memory isolation; MIG does.

notes.front: What is a GPU SuperPOD-style cluster?
notes.back: Many GPU servers tightly coupled with NVLink/NVSwitch inside nodes and InfiniBand (or remote direct memory access over converged Ethernet (RoCE)) between them, built to train one model across thousands of GPUs.

notes.front: Tensor processing unit (TPU) vs GPU: key design difference?
notes.back: A TPU is Google's application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) built around systolic arrays for matrix math: more efficient on ML, less flexible. A GPU is a general-purpose parallel processor.

notes.front: What is a systolic array, and why is it efficient for matrix multiply?
notes.back: A grid of processing elements that pass operands to neighbors each clock. Each value is reused many times while flowing through, so memory traffic is minimal.
notes.analogy: A bucket brigade: water moves hand to hand instead of everyone running back to the well.

notes.front: What is a TPU Pod, and what links its chips?
notes.back: Thousands of tensor processing unit (TPU) chips acting as one accelerator, linked by Google's Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI), a direct torus/mesh network that bypasses host CPUs.

notes.front: Why choose a custom AI application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), such as a tensor processing unit (TPU) or Trainium, over GPUs, and what do you lose?
notes.back:
Gain: better cost and power efficiency for a known workload at scale.
Lose: flexibility and the CUDA ecosystem.
notes.analogy: A purpose-built espresso machine vs a full kitchen: better coffee per euro, but it only makes coffee.

notes.text: Cloud providers split custom AI silicon into {{c1::training}} chips (throughput, large memory, fast interconnect) and {{c2::inference}} chips (latency and cost per query at low precision).
notes.extra: Example: AWS Trainium and Inferentia; Google tensor processing unit (TPU) generations also come in training- and inference-oriented variants.

notes.front: Where does a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) fit between CPUs and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) in the cloud?
notes.back: A chip whose logic can be reprogrammed after manufacture: custom acceleration (networking, video, some inference) where an ASIC isn't worth building.
notes.extra: Examples: AWS F-instances, Azure's FPGA-based SmartNICs (Accelerated Networking).

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: Why do large AI training clusters need specialized networking?
notes.back: Every step synchronizes gradients across all nodes (all-reduce). Network latency and bandwidth then cap scaling efficiency: the slowest link stalls every GPU.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What is all-reduce?
notes.back: A collective where every node contributes values, they are combined (e.g. summed), and every node receives the result. Used to sync gradients in data-parallel training.
notes.extra: Ring and tree algorithms (NCCL) keep per-node traffic roughly constant as nodes grow.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What is RDMA, and why does it lower latency?
notes.back: Remote Direct Memory Access: a network interface card (NIC) reads/writes another machine's memory directly, bypassing the CPU and OS kernel on both ends.
notes.analogy: Passing a note straight into a colleague's in-tray instead of handing it through two receptionists.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What is InfiniBand?
notes.back: A low-latency, high-throughput network fabric with native remote direct memory access (RDMA), standard in high-performance computing (HPC) and large GPU training clusters.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: Remote direct memory access over converged Ethernet (RoCE) vs InfiniBand?
notes.back: RoCE runs RDMA over standard Ethernet; InfiniBand is a separate fabric. RoCE reuses Ethernet gear and skills but needs a tuned, near-lossless network (priority flow control (PFC)/explicit congestion notification (ECN)).

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What is spine-leaf topology, and why is it used in datacenters?
notes.back: Every leaf (top-of-rack switch) connects to every spine. Any two racks are the same number of hops apart, giving predictable latency and easy horizontal scaling.
notes.analogy: Every neighborhood road joins every highway: any trip is local road, highway, local road.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What is bisection bandwidth, and why does it matter for distributed training?
notes.back: The bandwidth across the worst cut splitting the network into two equal halves. All-reduce stresses exactly that cut, so it limits training throughput.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: What does a DPU / SmartNIC do?
notes.back: A programmable processor on the network interface card (NIC) that offloads networking, storage and security (encryption, virtual switching) from the host CPU, e.g. NVIDIA BlueField, AWS Nitro cards.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: Direct-to-chip vs immersion liquid cooling?
notes.back:
Direct-to-chip: coolant runs through cold plates on CPUs/GPUs.
Immersion: whole servers sit in dielectric fluid. Immersion handles higher density but changes hardware handling.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: Why lay racks out in hot aisles and cold aisles?
notes.back: Rack fronts face a cold aisle and backs a hot aisle, so intake and exhaust air don't mix. Containment of one aisle improves it further.

notes.deck: Cloud Architecture::10 AI Cluster Networking & Datacenter
notes.front: Uptime Institute Tier III vs Tier IV datacenter?
notes.back:
Tier III: concurrently maintainable (N+1, any part serviced without downtime).
Tier IV: fault tolerant (2N, survives any single failure).
notes.extra: Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries bridge outages until generators start; both tiers assume that path is redundant.
